Carbon pricing and renewable-energy policy shape the investment environment. Financing conditions can influence the affordability and timing of renewable investment. Prior modeling shows that regional differences in capital costs can materially change decarbonization pathways \cite{ameli2021higher,calcaterra2024reducing}. The present study adds a framework for comparing fuel-price and inflation signals across regional WACC scenarios. A linked investment or energy-system model could extend the analysis to deployment and emissions.

Reliable energy finance is relevant to affordability and a just transition. European research documents substantial geographical differences in energy poverty \cite{bouzarovski2017energy}, and the OECD emphasizes aligning local climate finance with inclusive development \cite{oecd2021financing}. These concerns motivate analysis of financing conditions in Europe, China, and the Middle East.

China's energy transition also involves government intervention in energy markets. Policymakers could consider more market-driven price mechanisms, complemented by targeted green finance initiatives to reduce capital costs. State-supported financing can help encourage private investment in clean energy while preserving broader economic stability \cite{HE2017524,POLZIN20191249,duma2023risk}.

For the Middle East, dependence on fossil fuel revenues makes diversification important for long-term economic resilience. Policymakers could prioritize investment in renewable energy, with sovereign financing capacity providing a possible source of long-term capital \cite{karanfil2023energy,FATTOUH2013108}.

The urgency of mitigating global warming necessitates a rapid energy transition to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) \cite{messerli2019global}. Energy-system transformation is central to climate-change mitigation \cite{BOGDANOV2021120467}. This transition is not solely a technological endeavor \cite{CHEN20191564}; it also encompasses critical economic dimensions, among which the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is a critical metric \cite{BACHNER2019100373}. It represents the average return required by capital providers, balancing the costs of debt and equity financing \cite{BACHNER2019100373}. The environmental consequences of this financial indicator are profound; Ameli et al. report 35\% lower green electricity production in Africa under region-specific WACC assumptions in a cost-optimal 2$^\circ$C pathway; their financing-policy scenario allows Africa to reach net-zero emissions approximately ten years earlier \cite{ameli2021higher}.

A pernicious challenge for the energy transition is its inherent vulnerability to shocks from the legacy fossil fuel system it seeks to replace. Global oil, gas, and coal price fluctuations can affect inflation and financing conditions, creating potential exposure for capital-intensive renewable projects \cite{melodia2022energy}. Financing assumptions can change modeled investment choices and transition pathways \cite{egli2019bias}. Existing research has examined the relationship between WACC, interest rates, and unstable market conditions in the energy sector \cite{dobrowolski2022weighted}. However, less attention has been devoted to evaluating its influence on WACC within the context of energy transition projects. Additionally, the varied impacts of fossil fuel price volatility across different energy sectors and regions have not been fully explored.

The previous subsection outlines the calculation of $WACC_{it}$ using firm-level data, in which the cost of equity ($r_{Eit}$) and the cost of debt ($r_{Dit}$) are not static. They are profoundly influenced by broader market dynamics, among which fossil fuel prices play a critical role \cite{melodia2022energy}.

Fossil fuel prices can influence renewable-energy financing through several channels. Higher fossil fuel prices can improve the relative competitiveness of renewable generation, while renewables can provide a hedge against fuel-price exposure \cite{Lieberman2007RenewableHedge}. Stock-market evidence is mixed: Vr\^inceanu et al. find no significant effect of oil-price volatility on renewable-stock return volatility in their sample \cite{vrinceanu2020influence}. These observations do not imply a uniform change in CAPM $\beta$ across projects or regions. In India, Shrimali reports different risk and return profiles for renewable and fossil power portfolios \cite{su13052573}.

The cost of debt ($r_{Dit}$) may also respond to the macroeconomic consequences of energy-price changes. Fossil fuel prices are relevant to inflation \cite{melodia2022energy,millischer2024renewables}, and the interest-rate environment matters for WACC \cite{dobrowolski2022weighted}. Project contracts, counterparty risk, and risk-transfer instruments can affect financing conditions \cite{duma2023risk}. Evidence on environmental financial premia is conditional: Wilberg et al. find no association for aggregate ESG scores but a lower cost of capital for a stronger environmental component in their sample \cite{kjellevoll2023impact}. Green-bond issuance and certification provide an additional financing channel \cite{ehlers2017green,flammer2021corporate}.

Recent ACAIT proceedings include deep-learning studies of environmental and carbon-related forecasting. Xie et al. \cite{acaitXie2024carbon} study carbon-emission prediction using deep time-series models. Chen et al. \cite{acaitChen2023transfer} present a transfer-based adaptive recurrent neural-network model for enterprise carbon-emission prediction. These examples illustrate the use of AI forecasting for climate-related indicators.

In the model, the inflation rate is included as a crucial covariate. As a macroeconomically sensitive indicator, WACC is directly influenced by the prevailing interest rate environment, and inflation is relevant to monetary-policy and financing conditions \cite{dobrowolski2022weighted}. Additionally, fossil fuel prices themselves are closely correlated with macroeconomic inflation \cite{millischer2024renewables}.

This assessment model involves three fossil fuel prices (coal, natural gas, and oil) and nine types of energy transition projects. For each region, we constructed $3\times9=27$ separate regression specifications, giving 81 region--fuel--project combinations across the three regions. Coal and gas generation are retained as conventional-technology comparisons. The target WACC series are scenario projections derived from Calcaterra et al. \cite{calcaterra2024reducing}, aligned to 120 monthly rows per region for 2026--2035.
